**What I searched and opened**
- I ran two searches on the 1 April–30 June 2026 cap, covering unit rates, standing charges and network and policy costs.
- I opened Ofgem's 25 February 2026 cap update letter (the "Summary of changes" PDF) and read the cost breakdown tables in full.
- I did not open the Ofgem cost allowance models published alongside the letter. They may hold an electricity-only split, so that is where to look next.

**What Ofgem does publish**
- The letter gives the cost breakdown for a typical dual-fuel Direct Debit customer, on an annual £ basis: £1,641 in total, of which networks are £463 and policy is £106. The other lines are wholesale £652, operating/debt/industry costs £274, EBIT £42, headroom £16, levelisation £9 and VAT £78.
- Networks plus policy come to £569. That is about 35% of the £1,641 total, or about 36% of the £1,563 excluding VAT. This is a dual-fuel, whole-bill share, not an electricity unit-rate share.
- Ofgem's regional page and cap tables give the unit rate and standing charge for each region. A secondary site puts Merseyside and North Wales, which is the SP Manweb area, at 27.66p/kWh and 70.76p/day. I did not check that against Ofgem's own table.

**Why the whole-bill figure doesn't answer your question**
- Network costs are recovered through both the standing charge and the unit rate, and Ofgem doesn't split them in this letter.
- From 1 April 2026, Warm Home Discount costs move from the standing charge to the unit rate. Policy costs also fell by £130, from £236 to £106, after the Budget 2025 measures.
- Both changes alter the unit-rate share, so the whole-bill number would not hold for the unit rate alone.

items.text:
The finding that the loser is sideways rather than upwards is itself the main value. It turns a negotiation with five tiers of government into a short list of asks. Most levels can say yes because they give up nothing.

The default posture has a quieter strength the note understates: it needs nobody's permission. Roofs, diverters, private wires and behind-the-meter batteries need no new rule, no reimburser and no change from Ofgem. With the Welsh onsite-plant exemption running to 2035, the cell has a long and stable horizon to grow in.

Holding the flexibility sale costs nothing. Batteries and diverters bought for self-consumption keep their option value. If Bethesda turns out to be constrained, and R7 leaves that open, a revenue line appears without any redesign.

R8 also gives the sideways contest a ceiling. Network and policy costs make up about 35% of the dual-fuel allowance, and part of that is already recovered through fixed charges. A cell can therefore only ever shift a slice of a slice, which makes the roofless neighbour's loss bounded and so fixable.

items.text:
Building on the ceiling idea: the bounded sideways loss is also a design asset. Because the shift is capped and measurable, the cell can publish it, and a published number is something a funder can offset. That gives Option 4's fiscal ledger a positive role as well as a defensive one. The cell can show each level its own balance, and no other community energy scheme has to do that.

Value the note has missed is in the R9 lead. An SP Manweb plan entry that mentions Bethesda next to a flexibility-services item suggests the substation has at least been discussed. Nothing is confirmed, but it is a reason to expect the held option may pay, so buying diverters and batteries now looks even more sensible.

Rung 5 open as of right is also worth more than the note says. It gives the roofless neighbour a standing door, and that earns social licence. Councils and funders can back a cell that visibly includes the household with no roof.

Option 2 has a further benefit. A royalty tied to generation gives the community council a stake in consent. The council then has a reason to support the cell's planning applications, which lowers build risk for every later rung.

The finding that the loser sits sideways also gives the cell a reason to make its numbers public. A published, bounded roofless-neighbour loss lets a funder see exactly what they would be offsetting, which makes a royalty or community grant easier to approve.

The note also misses a timing gain. The note records 0% VAT on solar installs until March 2027. Roofs carry the cell's growth, so a deadline on their installation cost is a reason to build early, while the rung-1 and rung-3 capex is cheapest. Diverters and batteries bought for self-consumption also serve the held flexibility option at no extra cost, so the two cases reinforce each other.

The council precept sits untouched, and a council roof hosting a rung-3 lease also gives the council a visible role. Together with the royalty, that makes the council a participant rather than a bystander.

The default's weakest joint is its own equity clause. "Rung 5 open as of right, paying a cost-reflective network share" leans on a mechanism the note admits nobody has shown. Distribution charges are billed to the supplier, and no GB route has been found for an unlicensed cell to pay a separate share. If no route exists, the roofless door is a promise with nothing behind it. It closes, or it runs on discounted kWh that shift cost sideways, which is the Flanders pattern struck down in 2021.

Yellow's "slice of a slice" is not yet earned. R8 gives about 35% networks plus policy on a dual-fuel basis, with no split between unit rate and standing charge. The bound on the neighbour's loss is therefore unknown, not small.

Two moving parts could also worsen it. The RO transfer lapses after 2028–29, and a budget could reverse it sooner, putting the levy shift back. A regulator need not prove a cell harmful to resist rung 5. It need only point out that the cell cannot show it is not.

The Bill Discount Scheme, which the note cites as the nearest UK precedent for option 2, is funded by every bill-payer. So the royalty shape borrows a levy on non-members, which is the very sideways loss the ledger names. If the upstream reimburser is a levy rather than general taxation, option 2 moves cost onto the roofless household it claims to help. The note does not say which funder would pay.

Next, consent-linked money creates a planning risk. A royalty paid to a council that decides on the consent is exposed to the test for planning obligations: it must be necessary, directly related and proportionate to the development. A payment whose size tracks kWh generated fails that test on its face. A planning officer or a judicial review claimant could then argue that the council has taken a payment for a permission. Councillors who benefit from the community fund would also need to declare interests at committee, which the note never mentions.

The fixed-charge shift has a sharper edge too. Residuals now sit in standing charges, so the sum that moves onto non-members falls hardest on low-use households. These are often the fuel-poor, the cohort option 2 is meant to serve. Yellow's "slice of a slice" may be true of the bill and false of the people carrying it.

items.line: Regulation 122 of the CIL Regulations 2010 (as currently in force for England and Wales) limits only section 106 planning obligations that are relied on as a reason for granting planning permission, so a per-kWh royalty to a community council is tested only if secured by section 106 and not if it is a separate voluntary or private arrangement.

items.full:
Regulation 122 applies only if the royalty is a section 106 planning obligation that is being relied on as a reason for granting planning permission. It doesn't apply because the payee is a community council.

- **Text of the test.** Regulation 122 applies where a relevant determination is made which results in planning permission being granted for development. A planning obligation may only constitute a reason for granting permission if it is necessary to make the development acceptable in planning terms, directly related to the development, and fairly and reasonably related in scale and kind. The regulation defines "planning obligation" as one under section 106 of the Town and Country Planning Act 1990, including a proposed one. It also covers only determinations under TCPA 1990 sections 70, 76A, 77 and 79. The regulation is marked as applying to England and Wales.

- **A per-kWh royalty is caught only if it is secured under section 106.** If the developer makes a section 106 agreement or undertaking to pay the community council per kWh, and the planning authority could treat it as a reason for granting permission, the three tests apply. A royalty with no planning-obligation link, such as a voluntary community benefit arrangement, is outside regulation 122. The same is true if it is a purely private contract and the decision-maker doesn't take it into account. National planning policy and guidance say that unrelated voluntary benefits must not influence the planning decision. That point comes from my own recollection and I did not check it here.

- **Role of the community council.** Regulation 122 turns on the type of instrument and its use in the decision, not on the recipient's role. It makes no distinction for a payee that is consulted on, or decides, the consent. A community council in Wales is normally only a consultee. If it were also a decision-maker, a payment to it linked to the consent would draw more scrutiny on whether it was properly taken into account. I did not verify that point.

- **Which consent regime.** The regulation covers TCPA 1990 planning applications. Many generation projects of this kind fall under other consent routes, which this regulation does not cover:
  - In Wales, schemes of 10 MW to 350 MW are consented under the Developments of National Significance regime, and larger ones under the Planning Act 2008 process.
  - Smaller schemes go to the local planning authority, here Gwynedd.

  I did not check whether regulation 122 applies to the Developments of National Significance route; the regulation's text lists only TCPA determinations.

I did not look at Welsh Government community-benefit guidance. I fetched only the text of regulation 122.

items.text:
One alternative, worked through: keep the roofless door open but move it behind the meter, and pay it in money rather than electrons.

Black's sharpest point is that rung 5 needs a licensed supplier (R10), so the equity clause rests on someone else's goodwill. So stop routing the roofless member's benefit through the grid at all. A council roof or anchor host carries an array sized to its own daytime load, which is option 5's ground. Roofless households hold shares in that array, and the cell passes them the host's avoided-import saving as a bill credit or dividend. No kWh crosses the public network, no supplier tariff is involved, and nothing new is shifted sideways beyond the levy share that option 5 already accepts.

The royalty in option 2 then has a natural use. While it is funded, it buys gifted shares for fuel-poor households that cannot put up capital. That turns a lapsing grant into a lasting holding, which also softens Black's cliff edge.

Building on the share-dividend door: the weak point is that gifted shares are only as good as the array they sit in, and the host's own daytime load caps how much that array can usefully carry. The council or cell holds them in trust for the household, and they pass to the next tenant at the address rather than leaving the cohort. Building on the host's own meter: the rates risk Haiku left open can be designed out rather than waited on. Building on zero export and the cell-owned array: the untested point is whether a third-party-owned roof array counts as onsite plant. That can be designed around too, by letting the host choose between two ownership forms and picking whichever the rates answer favours.

Form A is the lease already described: the cell owns the array and sells output to the host. items.text:
Building on reading the displaced share off the host's invoice: the test can only price the cost the host's own bill shows, and a pilot pair gives one measurement, not a valley-wide figure. verdict.text:
As it stands, the default is right for rungs 1-4 and wrong for rung 5. Behind-the-meter growth needs no new rule, reimburser or flexibility sale. Paying the backbone is currently unproven as a mechanism: no GB route has been shown for an unlicensed cell to pay a separate network share on shared kWh, and the roofless loss is unmeasured, not "a slice of a slice". Rung 5 "as of right" would put the burden of proof on the cell and depend on a supplier's goodwill.

What each level takes is largely nothing, with the loss falling sideways. Welsh rates look exempt for onsite plant to 2035, but that reading is unchecked for export-heavy roofs. Treasury loses about £25 per member household in VAT, with no net model. The royalty (about £800 a year) has no reimburser and an unsourced capacity factor.

The run moved the roofless door behind the meter: zero-export host arrays, asset-locked gifted shares, and an annual published dividend-versus-displaced-share test. The pilot pairs a school (Form B) with a care home (Form A).

Still open: Bethesda constraint status, rates reading, invoice itemisation, funder type, and the fuel-poor bill effect.

Next check: open SPEN's tender-zone portal list for Bethesda.

lines.text: The question is this. A ratchet cell in Bethesda grows rung by rung: roofs, diverters, private wires, behind-the-meter batteries, and finally rung 5, which opens the cell to a roofless neighbour. What does such a cell take from each level of government and from that neighbour? And is the right default posture 'grow behind the meter, pay the backbone, keep rung 5 open as of right'?

lines.speaker: Sagredo
lines.text: Then start with the takings. Who loses, and how much?

lines.speaker: Salviati
lines.text: Mostly nobody above the cell. Rooftop and onsite plant has been exempt from Welsh non-domestic rates from 1 April 2024 to 31 March 2035, so the roof rungs take nothing from rates. The Treasury gives up about £25 a year in VAT per member household, which is roughly 2,000 kWh at 26p with 5% VAT, though no one has modelled the net position. The Yellow hat's point is that the real loser sits beside the cell, not above it. That turns a negotiation with five tiers of government into a short list of asks, because most of those tiers give up nothing and can simply say yes.

The snippets describe an exemption for 'onsite' plant and show no test of self-consumption or export. An export-heavy array on a council roof may well be rated. Your royalty is no sounder. The figure of about £800 a year assumes a capacity factor of about 46% that has no source, and it sets the German 0.2 euro-cent rate beside a pence figure without converting it. The true sum may be lower.

lines.speaker: Salviati
lines.text: I accept both points as they stand. On rates, the Green hat proposes fitting every host array with an export limiter set to zero export, and sending surplus to hot water or a small battery. That makes the plant as onsite as it can be, and so designs out the risk for exporting roofs. The £800 figure stays unsourced.

lines.speaker: Sagredo
lines.text: Set the neighbour aside for a moment. Is the behind-the-meter part of the posture sound?

lines.speaker: Salviati
lines.text: Yellow and Blue both say yes. It needs no new rule, no reimburser and no change from Ofgem, and the exemption to 2035 gives it a long horizon. Holding the option to sell flexibility costs nothing, because batteries bought for self-consumption keep their option value if Bethesda turns out to be constrained.

lines.speaker: Simplicio
lines.text: If, Salviati. Bethesda does not appear in SPEN's 2024/25 Market Prospectus (R7). The tender-zone list was never read, and the only lead is an undated Network Development Plan entry (R9). SPEN's 2025 round contracted 13.84 MW of the 56 MW it tendered, mostly at high voltage, and low-voltage contracts were rare. Meanwhile 0% VAT on solar ends in March 2027. That deadline pushes cells to rush into batteries sized for a market that may not exist in their valley.

lines.speaker: Salviati
lines.text: The run does not answer that. Its next check is to open SPEN's tender-zone list and look for Bethesda.

lines.speaker: Sagredo
lines.text: Now the neighbour. What happens at rung 5?

lines.speaker: Simplicio
lines.text: Rung 5 does not hold. Distribution charges are billed to the supplier. R10, which is itself unverified, found no route by which a cell without a supply licence could pay its own network share on kWh it sends through the grid. So either the door is shut, or it runs on discounted kWh that push cost sideways onto others, as happened in Flanders. If it runs through a licensed supplier, that supplier designs the tariff and can withdraw. You would then have a supplier's goodwill, not a right. A regulator can also refuse simply because the cell cannot prove the scheme does no harm, so the burden of proof falls on you. And 'a slice of a slice' is unearned. R8 gives about 35% for networks plus policy, on a dual-fuel basis only, with no split between the unit rate and the standing charge. Since residual network costs now sit in standing charges, whatever is shifted lands hardest on low-use households, who are often the fuel-poor.

lines.speaker: Salviati
lines.text: Blue agrees with you. As it stands, the default is right for rungs 1 to 4 and wrong for rung 5. The Green hat's response is to move the roofless door behind the meter. A school, a leisure centre or a care home hosts a zero-export array sized to its own daytime load. Roofless households hold asset-locked gifted shares, kept in trust and passed to the next tenant at the address. They are paid as credits against cell or council charges, so no cash changes hands, and no kWh crosses the public network.

lines.speaker: Sagredo
lines.text: And how would anyone know that the neighbour gains more than he loses?

lines.speaker: Salviati
lines.text: From the host's own invoices. Where network and policy costs appear as pass-through lines, the cell reads off the displaced share per kWh, multiplies it by the metered avoided import, and publishes the result beside the dividend. An array is built only if three tests pass: the host's load supports zero export, the rates reading permits the chosen ownership form, and the dividend at least equals the share displaced. The test is rerun every year. The pilot pairs a school on Form B, where the host owns the array, with a care home on Form A, where the cell leases it. The run also says to check the dividend against the fuel-poor households' own bills, not only against the host's saving.

lines.speaker: Simplicio
lines.text: Untested, every piece of it: the rates reading, whether invoices are itemised, the confidentiality of the contracts, the means-test question. There is also the royalty's funder. The Bill Discount Scheme is paid for by all bill-payers. If option 2's reimburser is a levy rather than general taxation, it charges the very roofless households it claims to help, and the note names no funder type. A volunteer-run council that plans its spending around that money faces a cliff edge when it stops.

lines.speaker: Salviati

One worry is partly defused: under R12, regulation 122 tests a royalty only if it is secured by a section 106 obligation, not if it is a separate voluntary arrangement.

# The ratchet cell's governance ledger — what each level gives up, and where every level gains

_Published live (2026-11-09). A follow-on to the ratchet cell (`NOTES-ratchet-cell.md`). The question: as a cell climbs its ladder, what does it take from each level of governance, from community council to the UN — VAT, levies, network charges, business rates, grid upkeep? And which designs, already working somewhere, let every level gain more than it gives up? This is a desk pass by one agent: about a dozen sourced lookups, no fleet and no independent adversary seat. Each option carries its own adversary, but the run has not been through the gate. Figures marked ≈ are orders of magnitude, not models._

_Moved on 2026-11-09 by a [world computer run](/world-computer?run=run-001): standalone hydro is rated but can get a discretionary Welsh grant rather than an exemption; the flexibility sale is now held back until Bethesda's constraint status is known; the royalty is made contingent on reimbursement; rung 5 stays open as of right; and the roofless neighbour's loss is marked as unmeasured._

_Moved on 2026-11-09 by a [six-hat run](/world-computer?run=run-002): "rung 5 open as of right" is replaced by a behind-the-meter roofless door (zero-export host arrays, asset-locked gifted shares, and a published annual dividend-versus-displaced-share test), and network-share payment, royalty funding and the Bethesda flexibility sale are now marked as unproven options._

---

## The finding first: the loser is the roofless neighbour, not a level of government

Go through the ledger level by level and something unexpected appears. **Most levels of governance lose little or nothing to a ratchet cell, and several gain.** The real cost of the cell falls sideways, not upwards. It lands on the household with no roof, no share and no club place, which ends up carrying a larger share of the fixed system costs that cell members stop paying per kWh. The walls ledger in the parent note already lists this as *network-cost shifting: political contest*. This pass gives it its proper place. It is the only line with a loser. Its size is not yet measured, and it should not be assumed to be small. Residuals now sit in standing charges, so whatever cost moves onto non-members may fall hardest on low-use households, and those are often the fuel-poor. A small average effect could still be concentrated on the most vulnerable. That loser is not a government.

So "every level gains" is the wrong test, or at least only half of it. It mostly passes already. The test that bites is **every level gains *and* the non-participant is no worse off.** The options below are scored on both halves.

## The ledger — what a cell takes, level by level

The take comes in three kinds, and they should never be added together: a **fiscal loss** (money a government no longer receives), a **reallocation** (a revenue-capped cost that moves onto other bill-payers), and a **gain**.

| Level | What a cell touches | Kind | Size and sign |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Community council** (Cyngor Cymuned) | Nothing. The precept is unaffected. | — | Zero take. Possible gain: a council roof can host a rung-3 lease, and the council can hold or channel a benefit fund. |
| **County** (Gwynedd) | Non-domestic rates on standalone generation (hydro, ground-mount); planning. Rates are pooled nationally in Wales, so the county keeps nothing directly. | Fiscal, small | Rooftop and onsite plant has been **exempt from Welsh rates since 1 April 2024, to 31 March 2035** (Valuation for Rating (Plant and Machinery) (Wales) (Amendment) Regs 2023), so the roof rungs should take nothing from rates. That reading is unchecked for export-heavy roofs. The operative text of WSI 2023/1229 could not be opened, and the snippets seen describe an exemption for "onsite" renewable plant without showing any self-consumption or export test. An array on a council roof that exports most of its output may therefore be rated ([R11](https://www.gov.wales/consultation-renewable-energy-rates-support-html)). Standalone assets (rung 7's hydro, any ground-mount) stay rated. Standalone community hydro is **not exempt**, but it may receive an application-based 100% Welsh Government grant up to £50,000 rateable value ([R3](https://www.gov.wales/non-domestic-business-rates-support-community-owned-hydropower-projects-2022-2023)). Guidance exists for 2023–24, but its terms are unconfirmed. Gains: lower energy bills in its own schools and buildings, fewer fuel-poor households. |
| **Welsh Government** | The rates pool; Ynni Cymru grant spend (rung 0). Energy licensing is **reserved**, so there is no tax or levy lever here. | Spend in, target out | A net gainer against its own target of **1.5 GW locally owned by 2035**. Every cell is cheap delivery of a stated objective. |
| **UK Treasury** | VAT at 5% on every displaced kWh; 0% VAT on solar installs (to March 2027); income tax on share interest; CBS corporation tax; the share of the Renewables Obligation it now funds. | Fiscal loss, partly offset | VAT forgone ≈ **£25 a year per member household** displacing ~2,000 kWh at ~26p. Offsets: taxable share interest, employment taxes on the paid officer, and lower fuel-poverty spend. Probably net-negative but small. Not modelled. |
| **Ofgem / DNO** (SP Energy Networks, North Wales) | Distribution and transmission charges per kWh. | **Reallocation** | The DNO loses **nothing**: allowed revenue is set by the price control (RIIO-ED2), so lower volume raises unit tariffs for everyone else. The transmission and distribution *residuals* already moved to banded fixed charges under the 2022 Targeted Charging Review, so cells cannot dodge them at the DNO-to-supplier level. How a member's bill shows them depends on the supplier's tariff design. What cells still avoid is the per-kWh, cost-reflective part. The **gain** is flexibility: a cell battery or diverter that defers reinforcement is cheaper than copper, and the DNO keeps part of any underspend under its totex incentive. |
| **Policy levies** (RO, FiT, CfD, ECO, Warm Home Discount) | Per-kWh levies on supplied energy. | **Reallocation** | The total cost is fixed (certificates and contracts are owed whatever the volume), so a cell shifts levy onto non-members. **This contest shrank in April 2026.** The 2025 Budget ended ECO on bills and moved **75% of domestic RO cost to the Exchequer** for 2026–29 (≈£150 a year off the average bill combined; ≈£90 from RO alone, per the government factsheet). That moves cost from a regressive base (per kWh) to a progressive one (general taxation). It is the largest single cut to the cell's sideways take so far, and it happened for reasons unrelated to cells. |
| **EU** | Nothing. The UK is outside; ETS linking and CBAM do not reach a domestic cell. | — | Precedent library only (see options). |
| **UN** (UNFCCC, SDG 7) | Nothing. | — | Takes nothing and can give nothing a cell can spend. Its only currency is attributable mitigation in the UK's NDC, which cells add to at no cost to it. |

**Read it upward:** above the UK there is nothing to negotiate. **Read it at the UK:** the Treasury's loss is VAT-sized and small. The DNO's is zero by construction. **Read it sideways:** the real contest is levy and network reallocation onto non-members, and the 2026 levy move has already cut it, by an amount not yet measured.

## The options

Each one is a design already running somewhere, mapped onto the cell's levels, scored on both halves of the test, and set against its strongest adversary.

### 1. Pay the backbone, sell the flexibility — the network level gains by buying what the cell can do

**Design.** The cell does not try to avoid network costs it causes. Members keep paying the fixed residuals (the 2022 Targeted Charging Review already makes that compulsory), and the cell volunteers a capacity-based contribution for any through-grid sharing (rung 5). The cell then *sells* to SP Energy Networks what it is physically good at: diverters and anchor batteries (rungs 1 and 6) bid into the DNO's flexibility tenders for the local substation, getting paid to defer reinforcement.

**Who gains.** DNO: deferral is cheaper than reinforcement, and it keeps part of the underspend. Non-members: lower reinforcement cost in their tariffs, and no residual shifted onto them. Cell: a new revenue line built on persistent value, which is exactly what condition 3 of the parent gate demanded ("price off self-consumption, avoided-network and flexibility value — the parts that persist").

**Precedents.** SPEN runs flexibility tenders across North Wales through Piclo/ElectronConnect: 113 MW secured at 12 HV/EHV sites in north-west England and North Wales in one earlier round. Italy's renewable energy communities (CER) reimburse only the *cost-reflective* network component on shared energy, not the residual. That is the right split. Germany's new energy sharing (§42c EnWG, live 1 June 2026) deliberately gives **no** network-charge reduction, on the grounds that shared electrons still use the wires.

**Adversary.** The tenders are thin and pitched at the wrong voltage. SPEN's 2025 round contracted **13.84 MW of 56 MW tendered**, mostly at HV/EHV. Low-voltage contracts, the voltage where a valley cell sits, are new and rare. Unless the Bethesda substation is actually constrained, there is nothing to sell, and the value per kWh may be pennies. Worse, Ofgem's *Energy System Cost Allocation and Recovery Review* (call for input closed September 2025) may push more cost onto standing charges, which cuts the unit-rate savings that rungs 2 and 5 run on. The backbone half is also unproven as a mechanism: the volunteered contribution for rung 5 depends on the same unshown route for paying a network share that option 5 sets out. Finally, the end of 0% VAT on installs in March 2027 creates pressure to rush into batteries sized for a flexibility market that has not been confirmed at Bethesda. Batteries should be sized to self-consumption. Any flexibility value is then a free option if the substation proves constrained. **Verdict:** passes both halves if the substation is constrained and a payment route exists. Otherwise it is a posture with no revenue. One query to SPEN's constraint maps settles the first condition, and that query has not yet succeeded (see next steps).

### 2. A per-kWh royalty to the community council, reimbursed from above — the German §6 shape

**Design.** Large cell assets (the rung-7 hydro, any rung-3 anchor roof over a threshold) pay a small per-kWh royalty to the community council. The council uses its general power of competence to spend it on the fuel-poor cohort the parent gate found the ladder cannot reach (the "false for the acute fuel-poverty cohort" clause). The decisive feature is borrowed exactly: **the royalty is reimbursed by the level above**, so the asset owner is neutral, the community council gains, and the payer is the level that wants consent and build rate. The royalty is payable only from reimbursement received and lapses to zero if reimbursement ends, so the asset owner never pays net. In substance this is a grant to the council, paid through a generation meter. The only reason for the per-kWh wrapper is that it ties the money to local generation, and so to consent.

**Precedents.** Germany, §6 EEG: operators may pay affected municipalities up to **0.2 ct/kWh**, and for EEG-subsidised plants the grid operator reimburses it. In effect the national surcharge account pays the municipality. Since the 2024 EEErtrBetG, projects approved after 31 December 2024 must pay (0.2 ct/kWh wind, 0.1 ct/kWh ground-mount PV, up to 0.4 ct/kWh for wind by agreement). The UK has now built its own version for consent: the **Bill Discount Scheme** gives households within 500 m of 43 new transmission projects £250 a year for ten years from 2027, funded by every bill-payer at roughly 80p–£2 a year. Wales keeps a register of community benefit (the £5k/MW onshore wind norm). None of these is a UK statutory account of the §6 kind. The German shape has no working UK equivalent yet.

**Who gains.** Community council: income it has never had, ring-fenced to the cohort the ladder fails, and a stake in consent that gives it a reason to support later planning applications. County and Welsh Government: progress on the fuel-poverty and local-ownership targets. Nation: social licence. Non-members: if the royalty pays for fuel-poverty outreach, the most exposed non-participants are the ones who gain.

**Adversary.** The UK has no EEG account. If nobody above reimburses, there is no royalty, and a reimbursement from GB Energy or Ynni Cymru is a subsidy for as long as it lasts. A future budget can end it, as it could reverse the 2026 levy move. The funder's type matters as well as its existence. The Bill Discount Scheme precedent is paid for by all bill-payers, so a levy-funded reimburser would shift cost back onto the roofless households the royalty is meant to help. Only general taxation avoids that, and the note names no funder type. Scale is small and its inputs are unsourced. The ≈**£800 a year** figure reads the German 0.2 ct/kWh as 0.2p without converting the currency. It also assumes ≈400 MWh from a 100 kW hydro, which implies a capacity factor of about 46% that has not been sourced. The true figure may be lower. Whatever its size, it is a real outreach budget for one valley, but no more. The community council is itself run by unpaid volunteers, so the parent note's "residual saint" moves rather than disappears. Reimbursement-contingent money also leaves a volunteer council exposed to a cliff edge if it plans spending around income that lapses. Planning law is a smaller worry than it looked. Regulation 122 of the CIL Regulations 2010 tests only section 106 obligations relied on to grant permission. A royalty run as a separate voluntary arrangement, not secured by section 106, is not caught ([R12](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2010/948/regulation/122)). **Verdict:** passes the asset-owner half unconditionally, because the owner never pays net, and no rung's rationale depends on the money. It passes the council half only while it is funded, and only if the funder is general taxation rather than a bill levy. The candidate funder is Great British Energy's community fund or Ynni Cymru, paying the royalty rather than the capex. To blunt the cliff edge, spend royalty income, while it lasts, on gifted shares in the host arrays of option 5. That turns a lapsing grant into a holding that lasts. If funding stops, the council falls back to today's position of zero.

### 3. Exempt the community, retain the commercial — the county finally holds a stake

**Design.** Split the rates treatment of standalone generation by ownership. Community-owned assets (CBS, asset-locked) get full relief. Commercial generation in the same county pays rates, and the county **retains** them instead of pooling them. Gwynedd gains real income from the big commercial projects it hosts, the cell's rung-7 assets pay nothing, and the Welsh pool loses only the small rates bill on community assets.

**Precedents, one per nation.** *Scotland:* Renewable Energy Generation Relief gives community-owned schemes (≥15% of annual profit to a community organisation) 100% relief up to £145k rateable value, tapering above. *England:* the Non-Domestic Rating (Renewable Energy Projects) Regulations 2013 let councils keep rates from designated renewable projects, protected from the April 2026 retention reset. *Wales:* onsite plant has been exempt since April 2024, so the roof half is largely done (subject to the unchecked "onsite" reading in the ledger). For standalone hydro, the Welsh Government has run an application-based 100% rates relief for community hydro up to £50,000 rateable value. It was announced in 2018 and extended for 2019–20, with Ynni Ogwen named as a beneficiary ([R2](https://www.gov.wales/100-rates-relief-community-hydro-projects); [extension](https://www.gov.wales/100-business-rate-relief-continue-flow-community-hydro-projects)). Its status on the 2023 list is unconfirmed: guidance pages exist up to 2023–24, but those terms were not read (R3, cited in the ledger). *Spain:* municipalities may voluntarily waive up to **50% of IBI** (property tax) and **95% of ICIO** (works tax) on solar installs. Many do, so the lowest level gives up tax by choice, because the local return is worth more to it.

**Who gains.** County: a retained income it lacks today. Welsh Government: delivery of the 1.5 GW target at the cost of a small slice of the pool. Cell: cheaper rung-7 assets. Non-members: neutral to slightly positive (council income).

**Adversary.** Wales pools non-domestic rates *on purpose*: it is redistributive. Letting resource-rich counties keep generation rates takes from the counties without wind or water. That is zero-sum inside Wales, which is the very move the option claims to avoid. England's retention mostly produced nothing, because the de facto onshore wind ban followed straight after. And a small community hydro may already sit under small business rates relief, so the relief half could be worth zero. The Spanish evidence cuts both ways: 38% of municipalities offer no IBI bonus at all. **Verdict:** the community-relief half already exists in Wales as a discretionary grant, so it adds little that is new. The one open question is whether Gwynedd can **retain rates from new commercial capacity only**, above a baseline, as England designed it, without taking from counties that have no wind or water. Unless retention is limited in that way, the option fails at Wales level. The Ogwen hydro's rateable value is still unpriced, because the VOA entry was not retrieved (R2).

### 4. Move the take from the bill to the tax base — the Dutch fiscal route, and why it was abandoned

**Design.** Close the sideways contest at the root. The cost a cell shifts onto non-members is whatever is recovered *per kWh* without being caused per kWh: levies and network residuals. Every pound moved from that base to general taxation shrinks the cell's take from its roofless neighbour, and a tax base is progressive where a per-kWh charge is regressive. The cell-specific version adds a published **fiscal ledger** for each cell: VAT forgone set against taxes paid (share interest, wages, CBS corporation tax) and fuel-poverty spend avoided, so the Treasury can see its own balance.

**Precedents.** *UK, already moving:* the 2025 Budget took ECO off bills and 75% of domestic RO cost into the Exchequer for 2026–29, under the Energy Independence Bill. *Netherlands:* the **postcoderoosregeling** (to March 2021) gave cooperative members in neighbouring postcodes a reduced energy-tax rate on their share of the cooperative's output. It was a direct Treasury-to-cell fiscal transfer. It was **replaced by a subsidy** (the SCE, from April 2021) because the fiscal route was complex and hard to target, and the first SCE round was fully allocated in about two months, which is waitlist evidence. *Belgium (Flanders):* the meter-that-runs-backwards was struck down in 2021 precisely as a regressive cross-subsidy. That is the counter-precedent this option exists to avoid.

**Who gains.** Non-members: most of all, because the shift onto them shrinks. Treasury: neutral-to-negative, but now *visible*, and the per-cell ledger turns an argument into arithmetic. Cell: unaffected or slightly negative (smaller per-kWh savings), which is exactly the spread compression the parent template already designs around.

**Adversary.** This option is mostly a description of what is already happening, plus a ledger. The RO transfer is time-limited (to 2028–29), and a future budget can reverse it. The Dutch history says tax-route support for cells gets converted into subsidy once it grows, and subsidy is the grant-dependence the ladder is built to avoid ("no later rung's rationale cites grants"). The fiscal ledger is unvalidated, and an honest one may show a net Treasury loss. **Verdict:** the strongest on the non-member half and the weakest on the Treasury half. Its real value is defensive: it puts a number on the "regressive cells" attack before someone else does.

### 5. The frame-breaker: share the electrons without sharing the wires

**Design.** Stop asking how to compensate the levels the cell takes from, and push value down the ladder towards rungs that take nothing. Behind-the-meter and private-wire rungs (1, 2, 3 and anchor batteries) use no public network for the shared kWh, so they shift no network cost at all. Through-grid sharing (rung 5) is where the reallocation lives. Reorder the cell's growth plan so its expansion comes mainly from roofs, diverters, private wires and behind-the-meter storage.

The roofless door moves behind the meter too. It becomes **host arrays** on council or anchor roofs, sized to the host's daytime load and capped at zero export with an export limiter. Midday surplus goes to the host's hot water or to a small battery sized to its evening load. Roofless households hold shares and receive the host's avoided-import saving. No shared kWh crosses the public network, so no supplier tariff and no route for paying a network share is needed. Hosts choose between two ownership forms:

- **Form A:** the cell owns the array and sells its output to the host below the host's import price, as a rung-3 lease. The cell's margin funds the roofless holdings, and the split is published.
- **Form B:** the host owns the array, outright or on a community-funded loan. It pays the roofless holdings a roof-partnership amount set as a share of measured avoided import. The payment falls with the host's load, so nobody owes for a saving that has gone.

Shares for fuel-poor households are gifted, asset-locked and non-transferable. They are held in trust and pass to the next tenant at the address. The benefit is paid as a credit against existing cell or council charges (building hire, a heating-support scheme), so no cash reaches the household. Whether that fully avoids any means-test effect is untested.

Each array must pass a **three-step pre-spend rule**, and failing any one step stops it:

1. Does the host's half-hourly import support zero export?
2. Does the rates reading permit the chosen ownership form?
3. Does the roofless dividend at least equal the levy and network share that the host's displaced import shifts onto others?

The dividend-versus-displaced-share test is rerun **every year on a published ledger**. If the displaced share falls below the dividend, the surplus goes to a holdings reserve rather than to new arrays, and expansion stops at any host whose load drops.

The displaced share is measured in three stages:

- **From the invoice:** read the per-kWh network and policy charges off the host's invoice, where they are itemised as pass-through lines, and multiply by metered avoided import. An itemised invoice is a condition of host selection. This yields the first measured per-kWh sideways cost in the valley.
- **A default rate for later hosts:** after year one, a published conservative default rate, equal to the higher of the pilot hosts' measured shares, applies to later hosts on bundled contracts. A host may use a lower figure if its own bill shows one. Dividing the displaced share by cell membership gives what each non-member carries per member household. A sunset review relaxes the rule if the rate falls below a floor and re-ranks hosts if it rises.
- **What is published:** only the derived per-kWh rate and the host's avoided import, never the supply contract itself.

The test also checks the dividend against the fuel-poor cohort's own bills, so that it asks whether a fuel-poor neighbour ends the year better off. The **pilot** pairs a school on Form B with a care home on Form A. One year then tests both ownership forms, the rates reading, the invoice reading and the confidentiality rule.

Through-grid rung 5 is no longer open as of right. It stays an option until a payment route is shown.

**Precedent.** The physics, and the German legislator's reading of it: §42c gives through-grid sharing no network relief *because* it uses the network. Italy, Spain and Austria went the other way and discount shared kWh, which buys uptake at the cost of the sideways shift. Bethesda's own evidence points the same way: the binding constraint is *generation supply*, not demand. The missing rungs are roofs, which are behind the meter by design.

**Who gains.** Every level, almost trivially, because almost nothing is taken. The default needs no new rule, reimburser, flexibility sale or Ofgem change. Funders and councils can check the published ledger without any of those being confirmed. Non-members: not harmed by behind-the-meter self-consumption beyond its levy share, which the 2026 move has shrunk, and the host-array door pays the roofless at least that share by rule. Timing: 0% VAT on solar installs ends in March 2027, which is a reason to build roof and host arrays early.

**Adversary.** Self-consumption is still volume that does not pay per-kWh levies, so the sideways shift shrinks but never reaches zero. Host arrays displace host import too, and the annual test exists precisely because of that. The door reaches roofless members only through hosts with steady daytime demand (schools, a leisure centre, care homes), so its reach is capped by how many such hosts the valley has. Four of its supports are untested:

- the rates reading for a cell-owned Form A array on someone else's roof (see the ledger);
- whether gifted credits avoid means-test effects;
- whether hosts' invoices are itemised at all;
- whether the confidentiality rule satisfies hosts' supply contracts.

The old rung-5 door is weaker still. Distribution charges are billed to the supplier, and no current GB arrangement has been found that gives a licence-free community group's through-grid shared kWh its own distribution charge. Energy Local-type clubs rely on a licensed supplier instead ([R10](#sources-checked-in-this-pass): from unverified understanding, not primary sources). A rung 5 held "as of right" would therefore rest on a supplier's commercial appetite, since the supplier controls the tariff design and can withdraw. It would also put the burden of proof on the cell, because a regulator can resist it simply because the cell cannot show it does no harm. If it ran on discounted kWh instead, it would repeat the Flanders pattern. **Verdict:** the cleanest answer to the governance question. On equity, it now rests on the host-array door, which remains unproven until the pilot year reports. Grow behind the meter by default. Open through-grid membership only once someone shows a GB route to pay a cost-reflective network share and what a roofless member saves after paying it.

## What I think

The question assumed the fight was vertical: parish against county against Westminster. The ledger says it is horizontal. Above the UK nothing is taken. At the UK level the Treasury's loss is VAT-sized and the DNO's is zero by design.
